body.text: Magnitude-4.8 earthquake strikes near Korumburra, south-east of Melbourne
In short:
A 4.8-magnitude earthquake has been recorded near the Victorian town of Korumburra, just after 2am.
Geoscience Australia cited almost 21,000 felt reports in the area.
What's next?
Victoria State Emergency Service said there was no immediate threat to the community and no action was required.
A 4.8-magnitude earthquake has been recorded near the Victorian town of Korumburra, the second time a quake has hit regional Victoria in a week.

Geoscience Australia said the quake hit at a shallow depth of 10 kilometres just after 2am, and the epicentre was at Arawata, near the South Gippsland town, which is about 135km south-east of Melbourne.
The federal agency's websites cited almost 20,000 felt reports in the area. There have been no reports of injuries or damage.
A 2.5-magnitude aftershock was registered near Leongatha at 12:25pm, according to Geoscience Australia.
Hadi Ghasemi, a geophysicist with Geoscience Australia, told the ABC it was one of the strongest tremors the region had experienced in the last two decades.
He described the event as a "shallow, moderate earthquake".
"The shaking was widely felt, close to the epicentre. It was a strong shake but I don't expect any major damage,"
"The epicentre was less than 20 kilometres north-east of Leongatha."
Mr Ghasemi says while aftershocks are possible today, their likelihood will decrease as the day goes on.
"Aftershocks are often a possibility and we have registered a magnitude-3.1 aftershock for this recent event," he said.
"Generally speaking, aftershocks, especially the larger ones, tend to occur closer to the main event itself. The frequency of the aftershocks decreases from the time that the main event occurs."
Geoscience Australia also confirmed that a magnitude-3.1 aftershock struck, also near Leongatha, just before 3am.
The quake came a week after a 3.9 magnitude earthquake in Victoria's High Country.
Residents woken near epicentre
South Gippsland Mayor Nathan Hersey — whose municipality covers Arawata, Korumburra and Leongatha — said there were no reports of major damage in the region.
"Like thousands of people across Victoria, I felt the earth move under my feet," he said.
"There's no reports of damage so far except a text message from a resident who said their old house shook so much that there was paint flaking off the walls.
"My family all woke up just after 2am. My young son came running into our room saying, 'What was that?'
"It was his first experience of an earthquake. Everyone woke up — we're only 15 kilometres from [the epicentre at] Arawata, so we're quite close."
Michael from Iona in West Gippsland told 774 ABC Melbourne that the quake rattled his house and startled his dog.
He said the earthquake lasted between five and 10 seconds at his home, located between Melbourne's south-eastern edge and Warragul.
"It was an enormous shake, the house was shaking, bed was shaking. The dog started barking — it was full on,"
"There was an aftershock as well, about a minute later.
"The amazing thing is, there's an earthquake warning system and I got a warning straight away on my phone."
South Gippsland a quake zone
An earthquake in September 2021, with an epicentre at Woods Point near Mansfield, registered 5.9 on the Richter scale.
Following that quake, minor damage was recorded across central Victoria and in Melbourne.
The University of Melbourne's Earthquake Research Group director Mike Quigley told ABC News Breakfast the 2021 quake meant many Victorians had first-hand experience of seismic events.
"You never know, when the ground starts shaking, how large it's going to become — there's that feeling of fear about how big it's going to be,"
"A lot of people in that region of 16,000 — and the million people that felt it [across Melbourne and Victoria] — have also experienced the Woods Point one in 2021, so that might have been familiar.
"In this particular local region [South Gippsland], there has been an ongoing earthquake sequence since 2009. There was a magnitude-4.9 earthquake — it's an area where seismicity is common."
Monash University earthquake geologist Dee Ninis said the 2009 quake was followed by a similar magnitude event about a fortnight later.
The same region also experienced a magnitude-4.4 quake in 2011.
"The area is known for several geological faults which first accommodated extension of the Earth's crust to form the Gippsland Basin more than 100 million years ago," Dr Ninis said.
"In more recent times, in the last 5 million years, these faults were reactivated to accommodate compression of the crust, resulting in uplift and mountain building."
Following the latest quake, Victoria State Emergency Service put out a statement saying there was no immediate threat to the community and no action was required.
"If you felt the earthquake, stay calm, check for hazards, and be prepared for further possible aftershocks," the statement said.
For earthquake related emergency assistance from the SES phone 132 500.
